name: Japanese thermal reconditioning

card.summary: Salon chemical-plus-heat process that permanently straightens treated hair; no trials found, heat and scalp damage are reported risks.
card.note: Permanent for treated hair; reported heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss.

quick.overview:
Japanese thermal reconditioning (yuko, rebonding) is a long salon process that uses a chemical to loosen hair bonds and heat to set the hair straight. The result is described as permanent for the treated length.

No clinical studies on it were found.
quick.mechanism: A chemical loosens cysteine bonds in the hair, then heat restructures them in a straight configuration.
quick.risks: Reported risks include heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss; new growth is not straightened.

lead: Japanese thermal reconditioning, also called yuko or rebonding, is a salon procedure that permanently straightens hair. People with loose to medium curls or waves use it to get sleek, straight hair that stays straight through washing and humidity, instead of daily flat-ironing. [1]

Wikipedia describes a non-coating chemical applied for about 15 to 20 minutes to loosen the hair's cysteine bonds, after which heat sets the hair into a straight form and a neutraliser fixes it; the full process takes about four to eight hours. [1] It is described as suited to hair that has never been chemically treated. [1]

Because it alters the structure of existing hair, new growth is unaffected and comes in with its natural texture, so the straight look is maintained by treating regrowth over time. [1] Reported concerns include heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss. [1] No clinical studies were found specifically on it.

chain: Chemical loosens the hair's disulfide (cysteine) bonds
Heat sets the strands straight and a neutraliser re-forms the bonds
Smooth, straight hair that persists until it grows out
angle.text: The procedure replaces a curl or wave pattern with straight hair for the treated lengths, so a sleek look no longer depends on daily heat styling.

infobox: Loose to medium curls on untreated hair [1]

paras: Wikipedia classes it with permanent chemical methods alongside relaxers, which break disulfide bonds using hydroxide substances. [1] Unlike keratin treatments, which add a coating and soften hair for about two to six months, it is described as permanent for the treated hair and takes longer in the chair. [1]
Aftercare described in the same source includes avoiding washing for three days, using moisturiser and sun protection, and waiting one to two months before dyeing. [1]

Hair's elasticity and shape depend on disulfide bonds in keratin, which chemicals can break and reform. [2] Perming uses the same principle: in 1938 Arnold Willatt's cold wave used ammonium thioglycolate to open the bonds, and a neutraliser closed them around the new shape. Modern perms use sodium thioglycolate for roughly 15 to 30 minutes before neutralising, and acid perms from the 1970s use gentler chemistry. [2] Thermal reconditioning applies this idea with a straightening step.

Wikipedia lists heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss for thermal treatments, and chemical burns and breakage for relaxers. [1] Damage from heat is described as irreversible short of cutting the hair off. [1] Early heat-based perm methods in the early twentieth century are recorded as having burned hair and scalp. [2]
The article's discussion of formaldehyde-releasing agents and cancer risk concerns chemical relaxers rather than the Japanese method specifically. [1]

timeline.event: Karl Nessler's early permanent-wave method uses sodium hydroxide with prolonged heat. [2]
Arnold Willatt's thioglycolate cold wave, a precursor of modern chemical hair restructuring. [2]
